title: Data First, Partner Better. Jennifer McIver on Legal Ops Benchmarks, AI Agents, and Pricing Reality Checks
author: Jennifer McIver

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: McIver redirects the cluster’s transformation framing toward incremental, bounded agent workflows and quick wins. She accepts practical AI gains with human verification and internal-governance bottlenecks, but is skeptical that near-term adoption will automate end-to-end legal work or overturn the billable hour.
qs: But I think you’re going to see that it’s going to it’s going to take off in those smaller bits more and more.
And I think that, you know, some of the big things like it’s going to kill the billable hour, that to me is where the hype is.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: McIver’s experience supports the narrower claim that agent-generated work still requires human verification, and she is cautious about end-to-end automation. However, she does not address associate apprenticeship, expertise reproduction, or deliberate training reforms, so her position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.
I’m a little bit on the fence on that one.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The excerpts encourage dialogue, learning and change but do not address whether legal AI’s benefits depend on organisational adaptation and human control. They provide no substantive evidence, prediction or argument on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: If you disagree with me or if you have any further questions, reach out, because I love, again, to have those conversations.
That’s how we learn and that’s how we’re able to convey some change.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Wilkins’s observations about job mobility, newly emerging roles and opportunity are consistent with a growing legal-tech ecosystem, but the excerpt does not assess vendor proliferation, product adoption, market consolidation, agentic claims or the need for disciplined procurement and implementation.
qs: We’ve seen so many jobs or titles or roles that didn’t exist even a year ago open up.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: McIver accepts the cluster’s bounded, human-in-the-loop account and adds concrete legal-operations evidence: a small agent produced time savings while still requiring review, and internal security, privacy and approval processes—not lack of client interest—were key adoption barriers. Her view that eliminating the billable hour is hype also reinforces the synthesis’s expectation of incremental rather than sweeping commercial change.
qs: I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.

I think the roadblocks have been internally, a lot of our clients have actual like AI boards or AI community or committees that they have to go through in order to even use AI in an existing solution.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: McIver accepts selective, workflow-level AI deployment and materially develops the operating-model side of the proposition. She identifies usable, centralised data and team capability as prerequisites, while limiting immediate agentic AI use to simple workflows; her claims are practical and experiential rather than measured evidence of productivity or quality.
qs: It’s centralizing your data, making sure that the data you’re collecting is usable data that matters.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: McIver supports the cluster’s cautious account of bounded agentic delegation: small, embedded workflows can save time, but human verification remains necessary. Her rejection of billable-hour extinction claims and uncertainty about end-to-end negotiation also align with the synthesis’s conclusion that current evidence does not establish broad autonomous transformation.
qs: I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.
And I think that, you know, some of the big things like it’s going to kill the billable hour, that to me is where the hype is.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: McIver supports the cluster’s emphasis on selective, contextual learning rather than exhaustive release chasing. She relies on an internal AI specialist and industry conversations to filter developments, while acknowledging limited engagement with external media. Her evidence is practitioner experience, consistent with the cluster’s caution that networks provide useful intelligence but do not independently validate broader trends.
qs: He keeps up with it and then I catch up with him.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: McIver supports the cluster’s cautious account of task-level automation: she expects AI to absorb some assistant and entry-level analyst work while retaining human review. This aligns with pressure on junior workflows and continuing verification needs, but she does not directly address apprenticeship, partner succession or explicit development funding.
qs: But I do think that you’re going to see things that you would have an assistant do, things that you would have an entry-level analyst do.
I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: McIver directly supports the cluster’s proposition that legal transformation requires usable, business-contextual data rather than merely adding AI tools. She also endorses selective preparation: KPI-linked dashboards, external benchmarks and a limited set of relevant fields, while warning that AI exposes fragmented, poor-quality data.
qs: And I think that that’s where you see the biggest shift is the folks that are getting in there and creating dashboards that aren’t just everything thrown up, but ones that are tying into their KPIs that are tying into their business strategies.
Everybody wants those kind of easy button, know, I’m going to use AI and you realize that your data is scattered and your data isn’t the best.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central operational proposition by locating value in integrated systems, consolidated information and streamlined workflows rather than technology alone. It does not materially address contextual agents, lawyer supervision or verification, and offers objectives rather than measured outcomes.
qs: and really being a partner to the rest of the organization, whether it’s us working with our clients on integrations, for example, between our solutions and other solutions to really pull that information together.
And that’s really what we’re trying to get to and make sure that it’s as automated and streamlined as possible.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: McIver supports the cluster’s bounded, task-sensitive account: narrowly scoped agents can save time while retaining human verification, but those gains do not establish end-to-end automation or wholesale business-model change. Her evidence is experiential and preference-based rather than proof of profession-wide savings, displacement or the end of hourly billing.
qs: I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.
And I think that, you know, some of the big things like it’s going to kill the billable hour, that to me is where the hype is.

kp.k: Visible, benchmarked data supports legal departments’ strategic contribution
kp.d: McIver argues that effective legal operations teams turn accumulated operational data into dashboards tied to KPIs and business strategy, combine internal information with external pricing benchmarks, and tailor visibility to legal operations, general counsel, finance and sales. She presents this as a way to demonstrate legal’s contribution beyond its perceived cost-center role, drawing on industry conversations rather than a reported systematic study.
qs: You can look at your own and you can know that we’ve increased, you know, law firm rates have increased, you 10%, 12%. But without looking at external data, you don’t know if that’s the right path.
When you’re looking at say dashboards or data, what the legal ops team needs and looks at is very different than what a GC needs to look at.

kp.k: AI adoption exposes fragmented data and excessive collection
kp.d: McIver says enthusiasm for AI reveals scattered, poor-quality organizational data. She recommends identifying where data resides and collecting fewer, more useful fields. Her implementation experience illustrates how overly demanding intake forms produce missing information or uninformative categories; her comparison of six or seven fields with 87 is illustrative, not a measured threshold.
qs: Everybody wants those kind of easy button, know, I’m going to use AI and you realize that your data is scattered and your data isn’t the best.
I might only need six or seven data fields to tell a really, really good story. I don’t need 87.
But no one entered the data, and they were wondering why. Or it was always other.

kp.k: Small AI workflows offer gains while retaining human verification
kp.d: McIver describes developing an agent that turns event notes into takeaways and internal communications, with her review still required. She argues that accessible enterprise AI enables efficiencies legal teams previously lacked resources or time to implement. This is a personal implementation example, not evidence of quantified savings or autonomous legal work.
qs: I have an agent now that I’m working on and I haven’t spent that a lot of time and it’s almost perfect.
I still have to review it, but it’s giving me the ability to get a lot of time back in a little bit of effort.

kp.k: Agent demand exceeds evidence for end-to-end autonomy
kp.d: McIver reports that a LegalOps AI agent studio ranked first in an informal poker-chip voting exercise at the Amplify user conference; no participant count is provided. She expects adoption in assistant and entry-level analyst workflows but remains uncertain about end-to-end negotiation, which she attributes to a colleague’s more optimistic view. She explicitly regards claims that AI will kill the billable hour as hype.
qs: And the top one was a LegalOps AI agent studio. That was the number one.
And I think that, you know, some of the big things like it’s going to kill the billable hour, that to me is where the hype is.
So I don’t know if it’s going to be a complete, let’s do the end-to-end negotiation.
But I do think that you’re going to see things that you would have an assistant do, things that you would have an entry-level analyst do.

kp.k: Internal governance constrains otherwise receptive AI customers
kp.d: McIver says her clients have been receptive to AI from the beginning, distinguishing interest from permission to deploy it. She identifies internal security and privacy concerns and approval through AI boards or committees as roadblocks, including for AI introduced into existing software. These are observations about her vendor’s clients, not measured industry-wide adoption findings.
qs: I think our clients have actually been really receptive from the beginning.
I think the problem or maybe the roadblock per se has been the understanding from an internal standpoint on the security issues, the privacy issues.
a lot of our clients have actual like AI boards or AI community or committees that they have to go through in order to even use AI in an existing solution.

kp.k: Rigid procurement processes impede pricing and staffing innovation
kp.d: McIver criticizes both rigid rate-control programs and the opposite approach of seeking proposals for every matter. She recommends discussions about budgets, risk and staffing, including whether lower-risk, higher-volume work needs senior partners. She argues that corporate legal departments initially need to initiate change because firms may simply comply with prescribed processes; host Marlene Gebauer instead emphasizes shared responsibility.
qs: there’s no movement because there’s no communication, there’s no transparency, there’s no proactive reaching out and really trying something else.
do we need to have that most senior partner on everything, right?

Are there certain matters that might be a little bit lower risk, higher volume that maybe we can bring in some different staffing and really do it differently to get it into a cost bracket that makes a little bit more sense, right, for the work?

kp.k: Panels evolve toward providers suited to particular work
kp.d: McIver describes excessive consolidation over the preceding five to 10 years as potentially channeling all work to large premium-priced firms without securing assumed discounts. She says external benchmarks can expose poor pricing for particular work and observes panels expanding to include firms and other service providers suited to specific tasks. Her suggestion that 80 % of spend probably already reaches recurring firms is illustrative rather than a reported aggregate result.
qs: If you go back, you know, five, even 10 years ago, there was that initial firm consolidation kind of, I feel like, era in legal operations.
And then you assume that you’re getting those volume discounts. You assume that you’re getting the best rates.
you see inherently in your data that 80 % of your spend probably is going to a good chunk of the same firms.
And that’s where other service providers are definitely coming into play.

kp.k: Value extends beyond discounts to jointly defined priorities
kp.d: In response to Greg Lambert’s concern that buyer incentives favor visible discounts over innovation, McIver recommends defining value and partnership rather than focusing solely on numerical spending comparisons. She says value is not standardized: priorities might include developing a more diverse attorney pipeline or collaborating on technology and AI. She also distinguishes premium-priced, company-critical matters from other work where clients should examine different forms of value.
qs: think too many people are looking at the numbers on a spreadsheet.
I don’t think there is a standardized what is value.
For others it’s how are we partnering together on technology? We know AI is going to be great. What can we do to partner?

kp.k: Partnership requires revisable fees and reciprocal performance feedback
kp.d: McIver illustrates partnership with an unnamed client using probably 80 % AFAs: either side can reopen discussions when an arrangement stops working rather than waiting for an over-budget invoice dispute. She also describes clients educating firms about their businesses through law firm days involving associates, and firms providing feedback on in-house responsiveness and scope clarity. These are practice examples and recommendations, not measured evidence of improved outcomes.
qs: working with a client that does probably 80 % AFAs
And if it just doesn’t look like that arrangement works, either party is reaching out and having that conversation.
they’re not just bringing in that relationship partner, they’re bringing in associates that are key on their matters.
Most don’t want to hear that, but when you hear that you’re not being responsive or you hear that you’re really, really confusing me on the scope, that’s going to actually drive better outcomes too.

kp.k: 2026 preparation centers on data, partnerships and team capabilities
kp.d: Asked how firms and in-house teams should prepare for the next three to five years, McIver recommends centralizing usable data, discussing operational and technology needs openly with providers, and examining team expertise in data and AI. She predicts that 2026 will bring redefined legal operations roles and changes in hiring, including attention to innovation and knowledge-management capabilities. This is explicitly a forward-looking judgment.
qs: It’s centralizing your data, making sure that the data you’re collecting is usable data that matters.
And that’s really going to be examining your expertise within your team.
And I think that 2026 is really going to be the year of redefining the role within legal
So I think you’re going to see a lot of shifts this year coming up in 2026 on the roles and how people are hiring.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McIver presents AI's immediate value as incremental workflow assistance rather than wholesale transformation of pricing or autonomous negotiation.
pts.d: At 13:16, Jennifer McIver says accessible enterprise AI and agent-building tools allow legal teams to automate tasks they previously lacked the resources or time to address. She predicts growth in workflows involving tasks performed by assistants and entry-level analysts, without predicting that those jobs will disappear. She regards claims that AI will kill the billable hour as hype and remains uncertain about end-to-end negotiation. Her personal notes-processing example retains human review.

pts.k: McIver says AI exposes weaknesses in organisational data, while adoption is constrained by internal security, privacy and approval processes.
pts.d: At 08:10, McIver describes attempted AI use revealing scattered, poor-quality data. At 15:35, she says her clients have been receptive to AI from the beginning, but internal governance and understanding of security and privacy have slowed implementation, including AI features within existing software.

pts.k: McIver predicts that data readiness, partnerships and changing skills requirements will shape legal operations' ability to benefit from AI.
pts.d: At 30:57, McIver predicts that teams neglecting usable, centralised data will lag. She argues that discussing needs with firms and other providers now will improve future AI partnerships. She identifies 2026 as a year of role redefinition and hiring changes, emphasising the skills needed to assemble data and use AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw principally on McIver's personal AI use, client conversations and an informal user-conference preference exercise.
pts.d: McIver describes an agent she is developing to turn event notes into takeaways and internal communications, reporting time savings without a quantified comparison or independent assessment. At the Amplify user conference, participants allocated poker chips to proposed innovations, and a LegalOps AI agent studio ranked first; this supports reported interest rather than demonstrated operational performance. Her adoption observations and forecasts reflect her legal-operations and industry-insights experience. The transcript supplies no measured AI productivity study, labour-market data or model benchmark supporting these predictions; the legal-spend benchmarking discussed elsewhere is not an AI performance evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Small-scale benefits are described as available now, further workflow adoption is an undated forecast, and role and hiring changes are specifically forecast for 2026.
pts.d: Speaking in late 2025, McIver describes current personal use and anticipates further incremental adoption as legal software enables it. Her example is still under development and requires human verification, not direct reliance on autonomous output. Enterprise-tool availability and internal approvals condition adoption. In response to a question about preparing for the next three to five years, she recommends action on data and partnerships now and explicitly dates her role-redefinition forecast to 2026. She gives no definite timeframe for autonomous negotiation and does not endorse its inevitability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, legal operations staff, law-firm support and innovation functions, and their provider partners.
pts.d: McIver frames AI as giving resource-constrained legal teams capacity and time savings, including through user-created workflows. Assistant and entry-level analyst tasks are potential automation targets, but she makes no explicit headcount-reduction prediction. Legal operations, innovation and knowledge-management functions face changing skills and hiring priorities. Corporate legal departments, law firms and other legal service providers need data readiness and conversations about technology and business needs to build effective AI partnerships. Her claims concern enterprise legal operations rather than access to justice or public-facing legal advice.
